I'm exhausted, but in a hotel and showed. It was a small crowd - with ~1000 paying people. (We got 50% of the door plus a base rate.)

I used to vomit before going on stage. Once, I even vomited as I was going onto the stage. I'd get nervous and even sort of freeze up at first. I wouldn't speak. I sure as hell wouldn't sing. I barely acknowledged that the audience existed.

But, I got used to it. These days, I'm very comfortable up there. I laugh and joke with the audience. If I make a mistake, I play through it. If it happens to be at the right time, I'll make jokes about it. I now sing. I now put on a performance - not just playing my instrument. People are paying good money to hear and see a show. So, I give them their money's worth.

In other words, you get used to it. The more you do it, the more it just becomes natural. I wasn't born to perform, but now I absolutely being allowed the privilege of entertaining. I can make them laugh, sing, dance, and even cry.

It's an honor. It's an honor I take very seriously.

And so, I've acclimated to it. I get up there and give them professionalism. I give them everything I have. And, truthfully, the audiences are usually way too good to us. That's sorta what happens when you get comfortable with it and start performing for large groups.

Tonight was small. They were close to capacity (a number of folks will get in for free, so there were probably about 1200 people). The venue provided security, which was nice. But, yeah... You'll acclimate in time. The gnawing sense of fear goes away and, pretty soon, you're looking forward to performing. You're looking forward to that time, because you cherish it. You cherish your chance to make the audience laugh, smile, sing, dance, cry, sit in stunned silence, etc... If you decide to take it far enough, you'll find you can even plan and take the audience on an emotional roller coaster by picking the music to create a certain theme. It's lovely - and a great honor that the audience gives you.

As a traditional-style pipe and drum band, we mostly play competitions, and we do a couple parades, a high school graduation, and some veteran memorial type events. The parades and graduation are fun because we actually get an excited crowd, sometimes just screaming in glee at us. The somber events are cool because you really see how deeply the pipes can affect people.

Piping competitions are really for other pipers, not an audience. There's usually less than 20 spectators for band competitions, and then there's around 4 judges who walk around us stone-faced with clipboards. We march in while playing, play one set, then march out playing something else, and stare at each other intently the whole time to try to stay in unison.

Solo competition, there's usually no audience, and applause would be inappropriate if there is. I just go stand in front of a judge who has a table and takes notes while I play with a blank or slightly annoyed expression on his face. I've figured out that this is actually the "listening intently to bagpipes" face and it doesn't actually mean they hate me. It was so weird the first time I competed, I was sure all my judge sheets would tell me, "Give up piping forever, you're hopeless!" Based on how annoyed they looked, and the brusque pointing out of errors I'd made right after I played. The judge sheets came back very positive and encouraging, though, and I even ended up with a 2nd place in Piobaireachd. (Well, really it's because only two of us showed up to even try for it, but that was another important lesson that kept me from quitting competitions.)

Looking at spectators is something I haven't gotten much chance to get used to, so it still throws me off. But competition has taught me to play through the errors, and I know the people at the park have never heard most of the songs I know before. If I mess up and switch tunes halfway through, they won't know. Now all I have to do is keep from totally blanking when I know I'm being watched :P

I'm gonna tell you a story - it might have something you can use in it.

Long, long ago, probably before you were born, I was taking formal lessons in classical guitar. And, I do mean formal. I was just a wee tyke and hadn't been playing very long. My behavior had been so poor that I'd been sent away to a private prep and boarding school. See, I test very well. On paper, I'm a fucking genius! ;-)

To make a short story long, a buddy of mine and I had wanted to take his dad's car to the dance. Now, neither of us was old enough to drive - but that didn't stop us from wanting to. After all, he'd let us drive it around the block a few times. We should be able to take it to the dance and pick up chicks when we cruised the strip!

No... The answer was a firm no.

So, we torched the garage and burned the beautiful Thunderbird to the ground!

As I said, I test well. Good thing, too. My father was a career Marine and my new destiny was the dreaded military academy. Fortunately, I test well! Also fortunately, my mother loved me. She sent my test scores to a very ritzy prep school. I was very smart on paper. So, they gave my family a discount and off to boarding school I went.

That boarding school was all the way in Maine. There are zero Marine bases anywhere near Maine. I saw my family very seldom and we did indeed grow pretty distant for a while. Eventually, I'd seldom even go home for breaks - including spending whole summers without going home at all. One summer, for example, I hitchhiked across the country a few times and saw a band known as the Grateful Dead a number of times. My mother, the wonderful enabler, used to wire me what money she could. Alas, not even career Marines made much money.

But, I digress... I figure the color is important. It's called foreshadowing, damn it! Read a book!

I'd been banging away on my guitar for quite some time, by childhood standards. My instructor was a strict, strict man - and mean! Oh, was he mean! He was meaner than the missus, and I'm pretty sure she's a bear!

Anyhow, I was to have my first recital. Unknown to me, my family showed up and was in the audience. My stern looking teacher was there. My classmates were there. My classmate's parents were there. It was a lot of damned people.

And... I completely forgot the piece I was going to play. I was supposed to play a piece by Bach, one of the fugues - BMV 2003 as I recall.

It should be noted that at such a recital, they know exactly what song you're to play. They know, so that they can judge it accordingly. The people doing the judging are, in fact, very skilled and well versed - they're also intimately familiar with the piece you're supposed to play. They know every beat and measure - possibly (and probably) better than you do.

I sat there, damned near in tears, and proceeded to play something entirely different.

I put my heart and soul into it. It'd taken me a few minutes (I'm guessing - it seemed like at least an hour but was probably only a few minutes, maybe even less) to get started. I forgot the audience was there. I concentrated just on my guitar. When I do this, and I'm not sure I can help it, I tend to look a bit like a cartoon character. If you're familiar with the Bugs Bunny cartoon where there's a pianist/composer then you have it pictured exactly right. Alternatively, in those same cartoons, if you're familiar with the overly exaggerated movements of a cartoon symphony conductor, then you also have it sort of right. The difference being that I'm seated and the arm movements are much less extreme.

And I played. I played the different piece (something from Issac Albiinez, as I recall) with all my heart and soul, with all my flourishes, and with gusto. I also played it pretty much flawlessly.

When I was done, the cheering was intense and the crowd gave me the very first standing ovation I'd received. The only one who was mad was my instructor. The rest, those familiar with the process, were very keen to tell me that they were very excited that I'd changed my mind and played a different piece. They congratulated me for choosing to do so and said things like Bach was just too stuffy for a first major recital.

I distinctly did not correct them and tell them why I'd changed. I accepted the lavish praise and the accolades given to me by my parents and my siblings. The other parents found it wonderful and were excited to have been there and to have their children be friends with "an absolute prodigy" (I'm nothing of the sort, I have to actually work to get the results I get.)

The only one who really knew was my instructor. He was livid but couldn't show it. By the time we had time alone, he'd calmed down. He was no longer angry and said I'd done the right thing and that I should note how the audience responded. He told me that I should remember it. He said that I had the benefit of them not knowing what was in my head. I had the benefit of being the one to make the decisions and not having to justify them.

At the time, I didn't get it. In time, I've learned to interpret those things in a variety of ways. Basically, if you screw up - just pretend it was intentional and play on with gusto!

One of the hardest things for a musician to do is to play through their mistakes. Every instinct we have is to stop and correct the mistake, sometimes by starting over. Fighting those instincts is important. I'm not sure how important, but it's important.

I'm not sure what you can take from that, but there might be something in there for you. I'm home (obviously). Our drummer will be here later. He's bringing the truck by. He's tasked with keeping our truck secure, getting it from Point A to Point B, maintaining the truck, and keeping it cleaned and organized. (He gets extra pay for this and is 'second in command.') I'm not sure how much assistance I'll render, but he is going to do a bit of maintenance on the truck and clean it.
